title: Ordinary Least Squares as an Attention Mechanism
claim: Three seemingly different formulations of the same predictor are equivalent, and a standard estimator can be read as an attention mechanism.
layout: 3 columns, top-to-bottom flow, double-headed arrows linking central colored view nodes
description: A three-column roadmap diagram with a white background. Each column has a rounded gray box at the top holding an optimization objective. A labeled arrow marked "estimation" leads down to a colored pill in the middle row. A second arrow marked "prediction" leads from the pill to a gray formula box at the bottom. The left column is navy and reads "coefficients-based view". The middle column is teal and reads "similarity-based view". The right column is red and reads "attention mechanism". Light gray double-headed arrows join the three pills horizontally to show equivalence. The top-left box minimizes ||y − Xβ||². The top-middle box minimizes ||y − XΩX'y||². The top-right box is empty. The bottom boxes give ŷ_j = X_j β̂, then a sum of inner products ⟨F_j, F_i⟩ y_i with weights ω_ji, then Q=F_j, K=F, V=y with softmax replaced by identity. The eye goes first to the colored pills in the middle row.
caption: Roadmap: Three equivalent views of OLS predictions. Left: Coefficient-based formulation. Middle: Similarity-based interpretation---predictions as weighted averages of training outcomes in a transformed space. Right: Restricted attention module with identity activation.
abstract: I show that ordinary least squares (OLS) predictions can be rewritten as the output of a restricted attention module, akin to those forming the backbone of large language models. The connection comes from viewing OLS as a similarity-based prediction rule in a learned embedding space. In this representation, least squares does not estimate coefficients per se. Instead, it selects an embedding that minimizes squared prediction error by matching training and test vectors through inner products. This maps directly onto the query-key-value structure of attention mechanisms. I then discuss extensions to dimensionality reduction, nonlinearity, and time series econometrics. Monte Carlo simulations and real-data experiments on UCI/OpenML benchmarks show that nonlinear Attention Regression performs competitively against standard machine learning baselines. In the reverse direction, I replace the attention sublayer of a transformer for tabular data with an explicit regression on polynomial features. The resulting model performs comparably to the standard transformer at a fraction of its parameter count.
